A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TAPS research and provide readable main text, figures, tables, and appendices A–F. Renamed configurations and renumbered exhibits can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original NLSI evaluations, tagging and tool-detection comparisons, manually annotated error analyses, and appendix tagger results.

after.justification: v3 retains these original empirical results and adds a controlled tag-corruption experiment in Section 5 and Appendix E.

M1.justification: The structured tagging procedure, joint-generation alternative, and least-confidence tool detector remain unchanged. TAG-S becomes EXT-TAG and TAG becomes JOINT-TAG; the appendix prompt contents confirm these are renamings.

E1.justification: NLSI interpretation remains the sole dataset and task. Section 5 adds a test scenario with deliberately corrupted intermediate tags, extending input-condition coverage without adding domains or datasets.

E2.justification: The baseline models, external and joint tagging comparisons, oracle configurations, and appendix tagger comparators are retained. New Table 3 summarizes existing configurations rather than introducing additional comparison methods.

E3.justification: The new sensitivity experiment randomly corrupts author-annotated gold tags at 0–100% in 10-point increments using deletion, boundary shifts, and semantic substitutions. Existing splits, model settings, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 5 introduces a systematic robustness study isolating tag corruption across three models and the full corruption range. Figures 8 and 11 directly test sensitivity to annotation noise, substantially extending v1's comparisons between taggers of different quality.

E5.justification: New Figures 8 and 11 display shaded bands around the corruption-response curves, absent from v1. Their statistical meaning and repeat counts are unspecified, so additional runs or a particular uncertainty estimator cannot be inferred. Existing correlation and significance reporting is unchanged.

E6.justification: v3 adds corruption-response results for F1, EM, precision, and recall, showing greater sensitivity for Mistral-3-Inst than the other models. Existing numerical tables and original plotted results are retained; for example, Llama-3-Inst TAPS remains at 51.18 EM and 83.94 F1.

T1.justification: The tagging representation and confidence-selection reasoning are unchanged, and neither version provides theoretical proofs. The new corruption-rate grid specifies an experimental setting rather than adding theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about tuning-free personalized tool use, structured tagging, selective tool invocation, and NLSI performance. The added robustness evidence does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5 extends the existing concern about tag quality into discussion of model-dependent noise sensitivity and conditions where tagging may become harmful. It additionally motivates compensating for noisy intermediate tags and improving entity understanding; the original limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 5 adds gold-tag annotation provenance and corruption-construction details. Existing prompts, optimization parameters, thresholds, hardware, runtimes, and code-access information are unchanged. The new study does not fully specify its sample, corruption sampling distribution, or repeat counts.

R1.justification: The cited works and substantive related-work positioning are unchanged. Related Work moves from Section 5 to Section 6 without changing its content.

P1.justification: v3 standardizes configuration and prompt names, expands ICL on first use, makes localized prose edits, and adds a sensitivity-analysis section and acknowledgements. Most existing prose and the overall narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 adds the configuration summary in Table 3, the F1 sensitivity plot in Figure 8, and three supplementary metric panels in Figure 11. Existing exhibits are retained with localized relocation, caption edits, and renumbering; page-number footers are removed.

improvement.justification: The controlled corruption study provides a useful direct check of tag-quality dependence, and Table 3 clarifies existing configurations. These improve evidence and readability modestly. The benefit is limited by unexplained shaded bands and incomplete experimental details. Section 5 also overstates monotonicity and the generality of harm relative to DEFAULT: Mistral's plotted F1 remains above its Table 4 baseline even at full corruption.
